# The Stirling bound for regular transformation semigroups

**Theorem.** Let $n\ge4$ and $1<r<n$. If a regular subsemigroup $S$ of the full transformation monoid $T_n$ is generated by maps of rank $r$, then $S$ has a generating set of at most $\left\{\begin{smallmatrix}n\\r\end{smallmatrix}\right\}$ elements. The same bound holds for a generating set consisting entirely of maps of rank $r$.

This gives an affirmative answer to Robert D. Gray's Open Problem 2, which asks to remove the uniqueness hypothesis on the maximal $\mathcal J$-class from his Theorem 18. The proof uses his bound on the cost of generating each principal factor. We combine those costs by matching copies of images to set partitions. [Gray, §3.3](https://arxiv.org/html/1307.8280#S3.SS3)

## 1. The cost of a single rank-$r$ class

Write transformation products in the order in which the maps are applied. For each $\mathcal J$-class $J$ of maps of rank $r$ in $S$, let $K_J$ and $Y_J$ be the kernel partitions and image sets occurring in $J$. Write $k_J=|K_J|$ and $y_J=|Y_J|$.

Within a regular subsemigroup of $T_n$, two elements with the same kernel are $\mathcal R$-equivalent. Indeed, for two maps $a,b$ with that kernel choose an inverse $b'$ of $b$ in $S$. The idempotent $bb'$ maps every point to a representative of its own kernel block, so $(bb')a=a$, and $a=b(b'a)$. The reverse factorization uses an inverse of $a$. Likewise, if $a,b$ have the same image, $b'b$ fixes this image pointwise and $a=(ab')b$, with the reverse factorization again by symmetry. Thus equal images give $\mathcal L$-equivalence. The converse implications follow from the ambient transformation monoid, where postcomposition can only coarsen a kernel and precomposition can only shrink an image. In particular, the $K_J$ are pairwise disjoint and the $Y_J$ are pairwise disjoint.

If $Y\in Y_J$ is a transversal of $K\in K_{J'}$, take maps $a\in J$ and $b\in J'$ with image $Y$ and kernel $K$, respectively. Then $ab$ has rank $r$, with the kernel of $a$ and the image of $b$. Consequently $a\mathrel{\mathcal R}ab\mathrel{\mathcal L}b$, so $J=J'$. Also every partition in $K_J$ has at least one transversal in $Y_J$, and every image in $Y_J$ is a transversal of some partition in $K_J$. To see this, start with a map $a$ and its inverse $a'$ in $S$. The rank-$r$ idempotents $aa'$ and $a'a$ are in $J$. They retain the kernel and image of $a$, respectively, and an idempotent's image is a transversal of its kernel.

The regular principal factor of $J$ is a Rees matrix semigroup with $k_J$ and $y_J$ the two index sizes. Its maximal subgroup acts faithfully on the image of an idempotent, and is thus a subgroup of $S_r$. Write $c_J$ for the number of connected components of its Graham–Houghton graph. There are no isolated vertices, so $c_J\le\min(k_J,y_J)$. By the upper bound in Gray's Theorem 7 (with the usual completely simple case if products never leave $J$), there is a set of elements of $J$ generating all of $J$ with size at most

$$
b_J=\max\{k_J,y_J,c_J-1+d_r\},\qquad
d_r=\begin{cases}1&r=2,\\2&r=3,\\\lfloor r/2\rfloor&r\ge4.\end{cases}
$$

Here $d_r$ bounds the number of generators of any subgroup of $S_r$, by the McIver–Neumann bound as stated in Gray's Theorem 17 and the elementary $r=2$ case. Gray's formula bounds the relative group rank by the ordinary group rank. Only its bound for generating the nonzero elements is used. A word yielding a nonzero element of the principal factor uses only elements of $J$ and represents the same element in $S$. All rank-$r$ maps of $S$ together generate $S$ by hypothesis, so it suffices to bound $\sum_J b_J$. [Gray, Theorems 7 and 17](https://arxiv.org/html/1307.8280)

## 2. Matching images to kernel partitions

First reserve all $k_J$ partitions of every class for which $k_J=b_J$. These reservations are disjoint. For the remaining classes we use a matching in the transversal graph. Its two sides are the $r$-element subsets of $[n]$ and all partitions of $[n]$ into $r$ nonempty blocks. A subset is adjacent to a partition if it is a transversal. No image of a remaining class is adjacent to any reserved partition, by the cross-class argument above.

Each $r$-element subset has $r^{n-r}$ neighbors. Its elements label the blocks, and each point outside it can be assigned to any labeled block. A partition with block sizes $u_1,\ldots,u_r$ has degree $\prod_i u_i\le 2^{n-r}$, using $u\le 2^{u-1}$. Hence every set of image vertices $W$ has at least $(r/2)^{n-r}|W|$ neighbors. If $r\ge4$, this is at least $d_r|W|$. It is also at least $d_r|W|$ when $r=2$ or when $r=3$ and $n\ge5$. In each of these cases, Hall's theorem matches $d_r$ copies of every remaining image to distinct partitions. Indeed, any collection of copies projects to some $W$ and has size at most $d_r|W|$. The partitions assigned to class $J$ suffice to charge its cost, since $k_J<b_J$, $y_J\le d_ry_J$, and $c_J-1+d_r\le y_J-1+d_r\le d_ry_J$. Distinct classes use disjoint charges, and none of these charges uses a reserved partition.

## 3. The case $n=4$, $r=3$

The four images are indexed by their missing points. A kernel partition has one two-element block. Identifying each kernel with that block makes the transversal graph the vertex–edge incidence graph of $K_4$. Any set of at most three image vertices has at least twice as many neighbors, since the counts for sets of sizes $1,2,3$ are $3,5,6$. If at most three images occur, the same matching argument works. It also works if at least one class has reserved partitions, since at most three images remain to match.

If all four images occur, each class has at least two images. Indeed, each class has a kernel partition adjacent to one of its images. Both endpoints of the corresponding edge index images that occur, so the absence of cross-class edges requires that both lie in that class. There is therefore one class with four images, or two classes with two images each. In the first case $k_J\le6$, $y_J=4$, and $c_J\le4$, giving $b_J\le6$. In the second case the kernels of each class can only be the single edge joining its own two images. Then $k_J=c_J=1$ and $b_J=2$ in each class. These bounds are at most the six available partitions in total.

In every case the sum of the local costs is at most the number of $r$-block partitions of $[n]$. The local generating sets supply the claimed generating set of $S$.
